# Math Refresher {#sec-math-refresher}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Appendix status: drafted.** Every mathematical fact the book uses, each with a
short refresher and a pointer to where it is used. This is a lookup table, not a
course — read the entry you need when the chapter that needs it arrives.
:::

The book assumes less mathematics than its subject matter suggests. What it
does assume is here, and [each entry is written to be enough to read the
chapter, not enough to derive the result]{.hl}.

## Linear algebra {#sec-math-linear}

**A vector is a list of numbers, and here it is a point in space.** A word, a
sentence or a document becomes a vector so that *similar* can mean *close*. The
whole of @sec-embeddings is that one move.

**The dot product measures alignment.** For two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and
$\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \sum_i a_i b_i$. It is large when
the two point the same way, zero when they are perpendicular, negative when
they oppose. Divide by both lengths and you get **cosine similarity**, which is
the dot product with magnitude removed — used everywhere from @sec-embeddings
to @sec-retrieval, and the reason a long document does not automatically look
similar to everything.

**Matrix multiplication is many dot products at once.** Multiplying a matrix by
a vector takes the dot product of the vector with each row. That is all a
neural network layer does, and it is why GPUs matter: the dot products are
independent, so they run in parallel. @sec-serving's prefill-versus-decode split
is a direct consequence — reading a prompt is many dot products at once,
writing a token is one after another.

**Dimensionality reduction finds the directions that carry the most signal.**
Singular value decomposition factors a matrix into directions ordered by how
much of its *squared magnitude* each accounts for, and truncating after the
first few gives the best low-rank approximation there is — that is the
Eckart–Young theorem, and it is why "keep the top components" is a theorem
rather than a heuristic. One qualifier that matters in practice: those
directions describe *variance* only if you centred the columns first. On raw
counts the leading direction is usually just the mean, which is why a
first component that correlates with document length is a sign you skipped a
step. @sec-embeddings uses it; @sec-clustering relies on the intuition.

::: {.column-margin}
If one fact from this section survives: **similarity is geometry**. Nearly
every retrieval, clustering and embedding decision in this book is a claim
about which points are close, and the arguments are about whether the geometry
matches the meaning.
:::

## Probability {#sec-math-probability}

**Conditional probability is probability after you know something.**
$P(A \mid B)$ is the chance of $A$ given that $B$ happened. A language model is
exactly this: $P(\text{next token} \mid \text{everything so far})$.

**The chain rule turns a sentence into a product.** The probability of a
sequence is the product of each token's probability given the ones before it —
$P(w_1 \ldots w_n) = \prod_i P(w_i \mid w_{<i})$. @sec-language-models builds
the whole subject on this line.

**Expectation is the average you would get in the long run**, weighting each
outcome by its probability. It is why a metric measured on 30 items and a
metric measured on 1,000 are different objects, which @sec-llm-eval turns into
sample-size arithmetic.

**Cross-entropy measures how surprised your model is** by the true answer,
averaged over the data: low when the model put high probability on what
actually happened. **Perplexity** is its exponential, and reads as "how many
options was the model effectively choosing between". A perplexity of 20 means
roughly a twenty-way guess per token.

**Softmax turns arbitrary scores into probabilities** by exponentiating and
normalising: $\text{softmax}(z)_i = e^{z_i} / \sum_j e^{z_j}$. Two properties
matter downstream. The exponential exaggerates differences, so a small lead
becomes a large probability. And dividing the scores by a **temperature** before
the exponential controls how much — high temperature flattens the distribution,
temperature approaching zero makes it pick the maximum. That is the single
parameter behind @sec-decoding, and behind @sec-machine-translation's
measurement that the same setting is right for chat and wrong for translation.

## Inference on measurements {#sec-math-inference}

This is the mathematics the book leans on most, because almost every chapter
ends in a proportion measured on a small sample. Four tools cover nearly all of
it.

**A proportion needs an interval, and Wilson's is the one to use.** The
textbook $\hat{p} \pm z\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$ breaks exactly where this
book lives: at $\hat{p} = 1$ it gives zero width, and near 0 it gives negative
bounds. The Wilson interval solves the same problem the other way round and
behaves at the edges:

$$\frac{\hat{p} + \frac{z^2}{2n}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}} \;\pm\;
\frac{z}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}}$$

Thirty out of thirty is not 100% ± 0; it is [88.6, 100]. @sec-llm-eval makes
the case, and most chapters after it report one.

**Paired data needs a paired test, and McNemar's is it.** When two systems run
on the same items, what carries the information is the *disagreements*: $b$
items the first got right and the second wrong, $c$ the other way. The items
they both got right or both got wrong tell you nothing about which is better.
The exact test is a binomial sign test on those discordant pairs, $2 \cdot
P(X \le \min(b,c))$ for $X \sim \text{Binomial}(b+c, 0.5)$, and it routinely
finds differences that two overlapping marginal intervals would call
inconclusive. @sec-prompting and @sec-llm-eval both turn on this.

**Anything that is not a proportion gets a bootstrap.** Resample the *items*
with replacement a few thousand times, recompute the statistic each time, and
take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. It needs no distributional assumption,
which is why it is the default for a ROUGE mean or an average rating. Resample
at the level the data is clustered at: two judgments of the same document are
not two independent facts.

**Power decides how big the sample has to be, and it is a question you can
answer before you collect anything.** For two proportions at significance
$\alpha$ and power $1-\beta$, the minimum detectable difference $\Delta$ needs

$$n \;\approx\; \frac{\left(z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{2\bar{p}\bar{q}} +
z_{\beta}\sqrt{p_1 q_1 + p_2 q_2}\right)^2}{\Delta^2}$$

which is the arithmetic behind @sec-llm-eval's finding that a hundred-item eval
set cannot see a five-point improvement. The useful direction is backwards:
start from the difference that would change a decision, and solve for $n$.

::: {.column-margin}
The failure mode all four are guarding against is the same one: a number
reported without an interval, compared against another number reported without
an interval, on a sample too small to separate them. It is the most common
mistake in this field's published results, and it is arithmetic rather than
statistics.
:::

## Optimization {#sec-math-optimization}

**A loss is a number you want to be small**, measuring how wrong the model
currently is. Training is the search for parameters that make it smaller.

**Gradient descent is walking downhill.** The gradient points in the direction
of steepest increase, so step the other way, by a distance set by the
**learning rate**. Too large and you overshoot; too small and you never arrive.
Everything else in training — momentum, Adam, schedules — is a refinement of
that sentence.

**Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to get the gradient**, computed
efficiently by working backwards through the network. You do not need to derive
it to use it; you need to know that it is what makes "training" a mechanical
procedure rather than a search.

**Regularisation is a prior belief expressed as a penalty.** Adding a term that
punishes large weights says *simpler explanations are more likely to be right*.
The statistical reading — a prior on the parameters — is the one that makes it
feel principled rather than arbitrary.

**Overfitting is memorising the training set.** The model gets better on data it
has seen and worse on data it has not. It is why every number in this book is
reported on held-out data, and why @sec-sequence-labeling's finding that 13.06%
of a benchmark's test set sat verbatim in its training split matters so much:
the held-out set was not held out.

## Notation {#sec-notation}

Every symbol the book uses, and where it first appears.

| symbol | meaning | first used |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $\mathbf{v}$, $\mathbf{x}$ | a vector (bold) | @sec-embeddings |
| $v_i$ | the $i$-th component of $\mathbf{v}$ (plain) | @sec-embeddings |
| $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{W}$ | a matrix (bold capital) | @sec-transformers |
| $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ | dot product | @sec-embeddings |
| $\lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert$ | length (norm) of a vector | @sec-embeddings |
| $\cos(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})$ | cosine similarity | @sec-embeddings |
| $\lvert V \rvert$ | vocabulary size | @sec-text-as-data |
| $d$ | embedding dimension | @sec-embeddings |
| $n$ | number of items, or n-gram order | @sec-llm-eval |
| $\theta$ | model parameters, collectively | @sec-language-models |
| $P(A \mid B)$ | probability of $A$ given $B$ | @sec-language-models |
| $w_i$, $w_{<i}$ | token $i$; all tokens before it | @sec-language-models |
| $\mathbb{E}[\cdot]$ | expectation | @sec-llm-eval |
| $\text{softmax}(\cdot)$ | scores to probabilities | @sec-transformers |
| $T$ | temperature | @sec-decoding |
| $\sum_i$, $\prod_i$ | sum and product over $i$ | @sec-language-models |
| $\mathcal{L}$ | a loss function | @sec-language-models |
| $Q$, $K$, $V$ | query, key and value matrices | @sec-transformers |
| $k$ | a count of things kept — beams, neighbours, documents | @sec-retrieval |

: Notation used in this book {tbl-colwidths="[22,48,30]"}

Two conventions worth stating because they are inconsistent in the wider
literature, and one collision worth warning about.

**Bold means a vector or matrix; plain means a scalar** — $\mathbf{v}$ is a
vector, $v_i$ is one number in it.

**$k$ is usually a count of retained things** — beam width
(@sec-machine-translation), neighbours (@sec-retrieval), documents (@sec-rag).
It is an index in two places, both of them sums over classes or samples rather
than over a vector's components: @sec-bake-off's macro-$F_1$ averages over $K$
classes, and @sec-embeddings' negative-sampling loss sums over $K$ negatives.
The distinction to hold is that $i$ indexes components and $k$ indexes a set
whose size is itself a parameter.

**$V$ carries two meanings and they are a chapter apart.** $\lvert V \rvert$ is
the vocabulary size from @sec-text-as-data onwards; $V$ unadorned is the value
matrix in @sec-transformers' attention. Nothing disambiguates them but context,
which is the convention the literature has settled on and not one this book can
fix on its own.
